CONGRANT.TITLE: Center of Excellence for Bi-regional Large Offshore Wind System (BLOWS)
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT:
The mission of the proposed Center of Excellence for Bi-regional Large Offshore Wind System (BLOWS) is to conduct research and prepare future leaders in floating offshore wind energy, to serve as a technical hub, and to develop best practices and innovative solutions to promote offshore wind energy at Gulf of Mexico and Great Lakes regions.

This work is proposed by a team of experts from four universities (The University of Texas Rio Grande Valley, Illinois Institute of Technology, University of Houston, and Iowa State University), two national labs (Oak Ridge National Laboratory, Sandia National Lab), industry partners (TPI Composites, GE Vernova, ), and one technical authority in marine structures and systems (American Bureau of Shipping). The four institution members have a long history of performing research on marine engineering, renewable energy and advanced additive manufacturing science and technologies that support renewable energy.

Our center differentiates itself by focusing on broadening geographic coverage to promote bi-regional collaboration. While many existing centers concentrate on regional or single-coast initiatives, our approach spans both the Great Lakes and Gulf of Mexico Coasts, which are not yet in the realm of geographic coverage of WETO, providing necessary research, technical support, and education programs tailored to solve unique atmospheric challenges in the two regions with a focus on floating offshore wind energy systems leveraging unique regional resources and expertise to drive innovation across diverse marine environments.

CONGRANT.TITLE: Ocean-based humidification-dehumidification desalination with self-sustainability
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT: An ocean-situated novel desalination technology is proposed. It employs a humidification-dehumidification (HDH) process to desalinate seawater. The process is completely and directly powered by nature, mainly by marine energy. Waves, tides, ocean currents, ocean thermal, and ocean salinity jointly function in a natural way to enable and maintain the HDH process. Winds and solar thermal further augment desalination production. The proposed research focuses on marine energy for HDH desalination. Wind and solar energy are auxiliary rather than necessary. Innovations of this HDH technology are reflected in both individual subsystems and the integrated overall system. The most innovative subsystems include a hydrokinetic heater and a humidifier. The hydrokinetic heater uses a hydro turbine to harvest hydrokinetic energy from water motion and directly convert it into heat, where the water motion can be caused by waves, tides, and/or ocean currents. The humidifier employs an array of wet cloth sheets to interact with passing-by hot and dry air for humidification, where the cloth wetting is maintained either by falling water films through wave overtopping or by natural wicking in lack of waves, and the salinity levels inside and outside the humidifier are balanced through natural diffusion. Upon integration of all the subsystems, the self-sustaining overall system is expected to produce freshwater in all weather conditions with zero electricity consumption (purely mechanical) and zero brine discharge (environmentally friendly). It will be a great fit for decentralized water supply at a low cost.

CONGRANT.TITLE: Wave-induced omnidirectional flow interaction with a vertical-axis unidirectional rotor
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT: The proposed work focuses on wave-rotor interaction, where waves induce omnidirectional water flows in the proximity of ocean surfaces and drive a vertical-axis rotor for unidirectional rotation. The rotor is a key component of a wave turbine, the latter being an emerging wave energy converter (WEC) technology. Unlike well-established wind turbine aerodynamics that deals with wind turbine interaction with unidirectional flows (winds), very little is known about wave turbine hydrodynamics that deals with wave turbine interaction with omnidirectional flows (waves). The main objectives of this project are to: (i) fill the knowledge gap in wave-rotor interaction through experimental study and, (ii) nurture more research on wave turbine hydrodynamics using obtained results. Ocean waves carry a huge amount of renewable energy that is largely untapped. While there are a large variety of WEC technologies under exploration in industry and academia, the wave turbine concept demonstrates certain key advantages and great potential. Success of the project will not only advance the wave turbine technology but also contribute to the sustainable development of coastal regions globally. The project will involve both graduate and undergraduate minority students in research. It will also promote STEM education in a coastal, cross-border, and Hispanic community.

CONGRANT.TITLE: ERI: Hydrodynamic and transport characteristics of water films falling down cloth substrates with grazing airflows
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT: The proposed work is on investigation of gravity-driven liquid falling films flowing over cloth substrates. The main goal is to gain fundamental knowledge on hydrodynamic and transport characteristics of the falling films that interact with passing by gas flows. In this type of two-phase flows, the falling films offer substantially enlarged contact aera and greatly lengthened contact time with the adjacent gas flows for effective heat and mass transfer. With nonporous and rigid substrates such as stainless-steel walls, falling films have very broad industrial applications and have been extensively studied over the years. With porous and flexible substrates such as cloths, on the other hand, very little knowledge has been gained. A novel application of the latter as proposed by the PI is to make seawater flow down vertical cloth sheets as thin films to humidify passing by airflows – a key process in humidification-dehumidification desalination. Other potential applications may include cooling of buildings, absorption of carbon dioxide, etc. Cloth substrates are very different in many ways from solid substrates, which will largely alter hydrodynamic and transport characteristics of the associated falling films. In this proposed project with focus on cloth substrates, we will conduct experimental research to: (i) identify such key differences, (ii) determine morphological evolution of the falling films, (iii) quantify the interfacial evaporation mass flux in correlation with the heat exchanging rate and, (iv) establish parametric interrelationships between hydrodynamic and transport characteristics. The project will provide an opportunity for minority students in all the levels from graduate to K-12 to participate in research in various ways.

CONGRANT.TITLE: Development of a vertical-axis unidirectional wave turbine for low-cost electricity
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT: A point-absorber-type wave energy converter (WEC)—a vertical axis unidirectional wave turbine—is proposed. The turbine has a submerged rotor with a hydrodynamically optimized blade shape and layout, an elongated vertical shaft reaching out of water, and a gearbox-coupled electric generator with data-driven power control connected to the distal end of the shaft. The turbine is supported by a floating platform, which is secured at the testing site through slack mooring. The uniqueness and innovation are reflected in the turbine’s operating principle: The turbine’s rotor performs unidirectional rotation about a vertical axis in omnidirectional water flows in waves. The unidirectional rotation makes the turbine wave-frequency tolerant. The vertical axis orientation makes the turbine wave-direction tolerant. Both features enable the turbine a very simple and robust structure with a low cost and long service time. This operating principle will augment the WEC family with a novel WEC type that contrasts with reciprocating WECs and horizontal-axis cyclic WECs. The turbine concept has been validated through extensive wave flume testing. Potential risks in PacWave testing may include water leak into the generator and accidental blade damage. Conservative and modular designs for long endurance and easy replacement will be pursued in collaboration with industrial partners. Two research centers from UTRGV and MSU will provide support with state-of-the-art fabrication facilities.

CONGRANT.TITLE: Faculty Seed Research Grant: Wave powered autonomous underwater vehicle
CONGRANT.SPONORG: The University of Texas Rio Grande Valley
CONGRANT.AWARDORG: The University of Texas Rio Grande Valley
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT: An autonomous underwater vehicle (AUV) can fulfill various missions in the ocean. While most AUVs are powered by batteries, their endurances are limited from a few hours to a few days only. We propose a novel technology that can enable an AUV to harvest energy from its surroundings—the ocean waves—for self-recharging to greatly lengthen its endurance to a few months or even longer. The proposed concept AUV is in a torpedo shape and employs a fully hull-encapsulated mass-spring-damper system (i.e., a direct linear electric generator) as its power take-off (PTO) unit. While in the recharging mode, the AUV surfaces and converts wave energy for electricity. Considering the AUV of a common size on the order of 1 meter, resonance of the AUV and/or its PTO, to be excited by ocean waves, becomes impossible in typical ocean conditions. In this work, we will realize a medium-fidelity wave powered AUV model in a bench scale and test it in the PI’s wave tank. This medium-fidelity model will allow us to explore non-resonant methods and approaches to enhance the AUV’s capability on wave energy harvesting. The research findings will augment knowledge in wave energy conversion, AUV development, system dynamics, and wave-structure interaction. They will also support our future applications for external grants to advance our wave powered AUV research.

CONGRANT.TITLE: Parametric study of a vertical axis wave turbine
CONGRANT.SPONORG: TEAMER program, supported by Department of Energy
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT: A wave turbine concept has been proposed in this research. When deployed in waves, the wave induced omnidirectional waterflow drives the turbine rotor into a unidirectional rotation about its vertical axis, which will in turn drive a direct electric generator to produce electricity. The unidirectional rotation of the rotor enables the turbine to respond well in a wide range of wave frequencies with no needs for frequency tuning. The vertical alignment of the rotor makes the turbine tolerant to the wave propagation direction. The proof of concept of this wave turbine has been demonstrated through a preliminary wave flume testing. The TEAMER funding will support numerical modeling and analysis, which are expected to yield an optimized hydrodynamic design of the turbine rotor. The results will be used to guide a scaled prototype development for a comprehensive future testing.

CONGRANT.TITLE: Energy transfer between waves and a unidirectional rotor in wave energy conversion
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT:
The main objective of the proposed work is to gain a fundamental understanding of the energy transfer process between ocean waves and a novel class of wave energy converters (WECs), originated and validated by the PI. The novelty and potentially transformative nature of this project derives from the joint effort of three approaches to reveal flow physics in wave-WEC interaction from the energy transfer perspective: experimental study, computational fluid dynamics (CFD), and phenomenological modeling.
This proposed research into harvesting ocean wave energy will advance the knowledge base on designing and optimizing WECs. Presently, there is a global effort to strive for alternative, renewable, energy sources. The oceans are a huge reservoir, largely untapped, of constantly renewing energy carried by ocean waves, known as "Blue Energy.” Tapping into Blue Energy presents its own unique challenges. The constantly changing nature of water flow in waves requires that efficient energy conversion occurs for all possible flow directions in a dynamic fashion. The research findings of this work will lay the foundation for WEC development and provide an experimentally-verified theoretical framework that will enable the creation of efficient WEC devices that maximize wave-to-WEC energy transfer and minimize the reverse. 
These novel WECs of the PI’s design have a rotor performing unidirectional rotation about a vertical axis in waves; that is in contrast to the reciprocating motion of most other WEC technologies. A basic rotor, consisting of both horizontal and vertical hydrofoil blades, is to be employed. The wave-rotor interaction will be studied experimentally using a laboratory wave flume, and theoretically using both detailed CFD modeling and intuitive phenomenological modeling techniques. All three approaches will be compared and will augment one another to obtain a full understanding of the wave-rotor energy transfer mechanism. Upon success, this project will make a huge impact in our ability to harvest Blue Energy. Using this proposed research as a platform, a new, collaborative model of engineering education will be demonstrated between two neighboring institutions on either side of the U.S.-Mexico border.

CONGRANT.TITLE: Ocean-based and nature-powered humidification-dehumidification desalination
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT: A novel process to desalinate seawater is to be developed through the proposed work. Specifically, an ocean-based and nature-powered humidification-dehumidification (HDH) desalination process will be demonstrated in a lab scale. Innovative approaches include: (i) a floating system directly situated in the coastal water with no seawater intake and no brine discharge, (ii) a fully nature-powered mechanism directly driven by multiple renewable energy sources with zero usage of electricity, and (iii) a unique humidifier design using cloth wetting and wave overtopping to enhance mass transfer. The enabled desalination plant will be simple, robust, and environmentally-friendly, and is expected to produce freshwater in both large and small scales cost-effectively to meet diverse needs. Water quality analysis will be conducted in parallel with the technological advancement. The requested funds will be used to cover expenses on: wages for three graduate research assistants, summer salaries for three faculty members (the applicants), materials and supplies for the lab-scale prototype construction and water quality analysis, small instruments for testing the prototype, travel fees, and indirect costs. The proposed project will contribute to accomplishing the objectives 1, 2, 4, 5 defined in Water Desalination Act of 1996 as amended by WIIN Act and the objective 5 defined in Desalination 2008, as listed in page 2 of the FOA.

CONGRANT.TITLE: Ocean-based and nature-powered humidification-dehumidification desalination
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT: A novel process to desalinate seawater is to be developed through the proposed work. CONGRANT.TITLE: ISRP: A self-sustaining process to get fresh water from oceans
CONGRANT.SPONORG: The University of Texas Rio Grande Valley
CONGRANT.AWARDORG: The University of Texas Rio Grande Valley
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT: The project aims to explore a new process to get fresh water from oceans. The process is to be fully powered by the oceans themselves by means of the temperature gradient and waves. It does not use membranes to desalinate seawater. It does not produce brine either. Rather, it mimics the earth’s hydrologic cycle to a certain extent. Specifically, above an ocean surface warm air gains high humidity through natural solar heating. Below the ocean surface the water temperature naturally decreases with increasing water depth. By forcing the moisture-laden warm air to circulate through a cooling path down to the cold ocean at a certain depth, condensation occurs and fresh water is collected.  The air circulation is driven by ocean waves. With the help of winds, inexhaustible moisture-laden air can continuously move into the dehumidification site, making large-scale fresh water production possible.

CONGRANT.TITLE: MSEIP – Enhancement and Improvement of Graduation, Retention and Success Rates for Hispanic Engineering Students
Energy transfer between waves and a vertical-axis unidirectional rotor
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT: This proposed research into harvesting ocean wave energy will optimize the efficiency of wave energy converters (WECs) thereby bringing them closer in line to other renewable energy sources. At present, there is a global effort to strive for alternative, sustainable, energy sources. The oceans are a huge reservoir of constantly renewing energy carried by ocean waves. This energy source, known as "Blue Energy," has been largely untapped. If funded, this project will make a huge impact in our ability to harvest this resource. The main objective of the proposed work is to gain a fundamental understanding of the energy transfer process between waves and a WEC. The constantly changing nature of water flow in waves requires that efficient energy conversion occur for all possible flow directions in a dynamic fashion. The research findings of this work will lay the foundation for WEC development and provide an experimentally-verified theoretical framework that will enable the creation of efficient WEC devices that maximize wave-to-WEC energy transfer and minimize the reverse. A novel class of WECs, originated and validated by the PI, will be the focus of the work. These WEC have a rotor performing unidirectional rotation about a vertical axis in waves; that is in contrast to reciprocating motion of most other WEC technologies. The rotor can have various types of blades (e.g. hydrofoil or hemispherical) that interact with the waves to produce unidirectional motion. The wave-rotor interaction will be studied experimentally for different types of blades using a laboratory wave flume, and theoretically using both detailed computational fluid dynamics (CFD) modeling and intuitive phenomenological modeling techniques. All three approaches will be compared so that a full understanding of the wave-rotor interaction will be obtained. Using this proposed research as a platform, a new model of engineering education will be demonstrated between two Hispanic-serving institutions through cross-border (U.S. and Mexico) collaborations.

CONGRANT.TITLE: An engineered hydrologic cycle for fresh water from oceans
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT: Two-thirds of the world’s population face severe water scarcity (Sci. Adv. 2, e1500323, ’16). Existing desalination technologies (e.g., membrane-based, thermal-based, etc.) have various drawbacks on scale up, energy consumption, water quality, and environmental impact (Water Res., 75, 164, ’15). Emerging technologies for collection of airborne water are limited to small-scale production (Science, 356, 430, ’17). Mother Nature feeds the globe with freshwater by extracting it from oceans through the hydrologic cycle (HC) – evaporation, condensation, and precipitation. We propose an engineering research project to engineer the HC at an ocean site for utility-scale freshwater production. Simply put, moist warm air over the ocean surface continuously enters a downward flow passage and reaches a certain water depth, where the air is naturally cooled by chilled ocean water and the airborne water is collected through condensation. The cold dry air then runs through an upward flow passage, escapes at the warm ocean surface, and recovers temperature and humidity. The uniqueness is on realizing a fully nature-powered engineered HC: winds to feed the site with inexhaustible moisture-laden air, waves to drive the air through the flow passage, the temperature gradient of the ocean water to provide cooling for condensation, and the solar energy to power humidity replenishment.

CONGRANT.TITLE: NSF-MRI: Acquisition of Micro Particle Velocimetry (micro-PIV) System for Microfluidics and Biomedical Applications
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT:
PROJECT SUMMARY
This proposal is for the acquisition of a Micro-Particle Image Velocimetry (micro-PIV) system to conduct micro-fluidics, MEMS (micro-electro-mechanical-systems), and biomedical flow experiments for both research and student training at the University of Texas at Brownsville (UTB). UTB is a minority-serving institution in the Rio Grande Valley (RGV) of Texas.  With a population of 1.5 million, comprised primarily of Hispanics, the RGV is the fourth-largest populated region in the state. UTB is the only institution in the RGV that offers both engineering physics and engineering technology programs. The RGV, a historically underrepresented region, presently has no micro-PIV systems to support science and engineering students. The MRI investment would provide promising young investigators with the resources required to greatly raise the stature of research in the RGV, attract new sources of research support, and elevate MEMS and biomedical education for Hispanic students to a competitive level. 
Intellectual Merit 
The project supports four specific research components detailed in this proposal. The titles and intellectual merits of these research activities are as follows: (i) Integration of Microcantilever with AC Electrokinetics  for Sensing Bio-/Nano-Particles.  This activity will result in an improved fundamental understanding of the AC Electrokinetics mechanism in complex electrode patterns and sensing bio-/nano-particles. Experiments using the micro-PIV system will further the understanding of electrochemistry at electrode/electrolyte interfaces in non-uniform AC fields and the interplay between bioparticles and AC electric fields for the implementation of high-efficiency bioparticle collection and separation. (ii) Biased AC Electroosmosis Micropump for Water Management in PEM Fuel Cells. This activity will use the micro-PIV system in research related to vortices in novel biased AC electroosmotic micropumps. This fundamental study is important to understanding fluid mixing and enhancing the efficiency of pumping in micro-channels. (iii) Biomimetic Flow Sensing.  The main objective of this activity is to obtain the micro-scale time-dependent flow structures, and to correlate them with a canal Biomimetic Neuromast (BN) response under comparable conditions. (iv) Selective Filtration/Absorption of Nano- and Micron- Size Particles Using Carbon Nanotube-Based Media.  This activity will synthesize carbon nanotube-based media with various morphologies and densities to selectively filter nano- and micron-size particles from fluid flow. Major advances will mainly depend on finding solutions to multidisciplinary research areas. 
The broader impact of the proposed research activities stems from the infrastructure enhancement that the micro-PIV system acquisition would mean to the MEMS and biomimetic laboratory of the UTB Engineering Department.  The acquisition would support current research projects and supplement some of our existing advanced equipment, resulting in more efficient and effective use. The proposed project will prepare qualified, skilled graduate and undergraduate students interested in multidisciplinary research. The PIs will engage undergraduate/graduate students in research and thesis projects. Academic enrichment includes student training based on investigation and characterization of interdisciplinary class projects. One of the objectives for the student training is to encourage undergraduate/graduate students to continue their doctoral studies at appropriate institutions.  Because a large percentage of women in the RGV lack a college diploma in science and engineering, women from the local, underrepresented Hispanic population will be recruited to become researchers. The project will help to improve measurement and instrumentation skills while introducing students to exciting research areas in MEMS design, micro-fluidics and biomimetics. The micro-PIV system will be used to demonstrate fluid flow in micropumps and to analyze data in MEMS/biological sensors for NSF-REU; and to provide research exposure for visiting summer high school students, motivating them to choose careers in science and engineering.  Faculty discussions related to the proposed micro-PIV system and its use have fostered growing interest from other fields, particularly biological sciences.  This project has great potential for interdisciplinary research and collaboration.  The project will enhance UTB’s research program and will be available for up to 20 students’ senior design and thesis research projects within the next five years.
Classification: UTB is a non-Ph.D.-granting institution and a minority-serving university.

CONGRANT.TITLE: MRI: Acquisition of subsystems to upgrade an existing planar PIV to a tomographic PIV for multidisciplinary research and education
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT: This proposal is for acquisition of subsystems to upgrade a previously-acquired planar (2D) Particle Image Velocimetry (PIV) system to a tomographic (3D) PIV.  Such an upgrade is commercially available; no further development effort is needed.  PIV is an optical method to measure instantaneous velocity fields and other properties in fluids.  Due to the highly modular structure, the upgraded PIV system will allow easy interchange between 2D velocimetry (the existing function) and 3D velocimetry (the augmented function).  This proposed new 3D PIV system will support multidisciplinary research of four faculty members from two departments at the University of Texas at Brownsville (UTB).  Four research areas, two in mechanical engineering and two in environmental sciences, will be greatly facilitated by the 3D PIV.  The four areas include energy harvesting from ocean waves, flow-cylinder interaction, interchange of salinity in mixing flows in an estuary, and water quality study.  To take full advantage of this state-of-the-art instrument, a PIV club for broadened research training will be formed, and a 3D PIV demonstration experiment for an undergraduate lab course will be developed.  A systematic approach will be to use the PIV demonstration as a forerunner and the PIV club as a bridge to integrate all the PIV-enabled research with education in both science and engineering at UTB (a minority-serving institution).

CONGRANT.TITLE: DURIP:    Build a wind-riding small drone with morphing wings for multi-agent collaborative learning
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT:
We propose a solution to kill two birds with one stone: develop a morphing wing for drones to ride winds and save battery life. We will mimic bat wings to achieve desired aerodynamic performance through a simple, light, and easy-to-maneuver mechanical design; artificial muscle fibers will replace traditional motors for actuation.  We vision that the drone can extend its wings to glide like a bird when wind is favorable. When wind is not favorable, the wings will be stretched in. With increased flight time, small drones are suitable for real world applications. 
Furthermore, we propose to enable the intelligence of drones by developing algorithms in computer vision, target recognition and multi-agent collaborative learning. Our goal is to explore the low space (<400m altitude) where we see countless applications directly benefiting human life: photography, transportation, surveillance, etc.

CONGRANT.TITLE: ARPA-E IDEAS: A vertical axis wave turbine
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT: A vertical axis wave turbine that performs unidirectional rotary motion in omnidirectional water flows is proposed for wave energy harvesting. This new concept circumvents common wave-energy-converter (WEC) issues such as poor wave-frequency independency of reciprocating WECs, poor wave-direction independency of non-heave WECs, and poor irregular-wave responsiveness of most WECs. Upon success, the new technology will demonstrate a strong potential to produce cost-competitive electricity from ocean waves.

CONGRANT.TITLE: RUI: Hydrodynamic characterization of a rotor in waves for unidirectional rotary motion
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT: This RUI project contributes to energy harvesting from ocean waves by advancing knowledge in hydrodynamics of a wave-driven rotor.  Ocean waves can directly drive wave energy converters (WECs) to perform two types of motion – reciprocating motion and unidirectional rotary motion.  In general, the efficiency of a reciprocating WEC is strongly wave-frequency dependent, whereas the efficiency of a rotary WEC can be somewhat wave-frequency independent.  To date, a huge majority of WEC technologies under development in industry belong to the reciprocating class, whereas only a few WEC concepts fall in the unidirectional rotary class.  In this research, a new wave-driven rotor for unidirectional rotary motion is proposed. To characterize the rotor performance and gain fundamental understanding of wave-rotor interaction, a systematic experimental study will be conducted in a wave tank.  Multiple experimental methods (particle image velocimetry [PIV], hot film anemometry [HFA], loading cells, and accelerometers) will be employed to reveal the flow physics from different perspectives.  To integrate this wave energy research with undergraduate education, a bench-scale rotor-equipped WEC will be iteratively developed by a large number of undergraduate students in parallel with, and guided by, the hydrodynamic research.  Specifically, students will contribute to the prototype WEC development by doing WEC-related design projects which will be implemented in a series of engineering courses.

CONGRANT.SPONORG: The University of Texas at Brownsville
CONGRANT.AWARDORG: The University of Texas Rio Grande Valley
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT: The fellowship supported proof-of-concept research of a new wave energy converter. The produced preliminary results were used in external grant applications.

CONGRANT.TITLE: CAREER: Wave interaction with a direct-drive rotor for unidirectional rotary motion
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT: This CAREER project contributes to energy harvesting from ocean waves by advancing the knowledge of wave interaction with a direct-drive rotor.  Ocean waves can directly drive wave energy converters (WECs) to perform two types of motion – reciprocating motion and unidirectional rotary motion.  Analysis shows that unidirectional rotary motion is advantageous over reciprocating motion in achieving high efficiency.  However, a huge majority of WEC concepts/technologies belong to the reciprocating class.  Only a very few concepts have been presented—but no actual technologies have ever been developed—in the unidirectional rotary class.  In this research, a direct-drive rotor is proposed to realize unidirectional rotary motion in waves.  To gain fundamental understanding of wave-rotor interaction, a systematic experimental study will be conducted in a wave tank.  A rotor with simple blades (cylindrical shells of semicircular cross section) will be explored at different degrees of freedom and under a wide range of wave and rotor parameters.  Multiple experimental methods (particle image velocimetry [PIV], hot film anemometry [HFA], loading cells, and accelerometers) will be employed to reveal the flow physics from different perspectives.  In addition, a bench-scale rotor-instrumented WEC will be iteratively developed in parallel with, and guided by, the wave-rotor interaction research.  This WEC development is intended to create a platform that promotes integration of research and education in multiple schemes under the theme of wave energy harvesting; it is all to be accomplished by undergraduate students.

CONGRANT.TITLE: Collaborative Research: A fully-shielded and free-floating wave energy converter with low maintenance demand
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT:
This research proposes an innovative wave energy converter (WEC) architecture for energy harvesting from ocean waves.  The proposed WEC is free-floating over the ocean surface and converts the wave motion to electricity.  The scavenged electricity is transmitted to a nearby base station wirelessly, and then delivered to an onshore power station via an undersea cable.  The proposed WEC is fully-shielded and hence is free from seawater corrosion.  In addition, it employs a highly-robust wave-riding mechanism.  As a result, it requires little maintenance for at least five years.  Its success is expected to significantly lower the high maintenance cost associated with wave energy harvesting.  The objective of this research is to verify the feasibility of the proposed WEC architecture.  It includes the following three major tasks.
Task A: 	To study the hydrodynamic characteristics of free-floating and fully-sealed WECs comprehensively.
Task B: 	To investigate efficient wireless power transmission schemes between a wave-riding WEC and a stationary base station, by taking advantage of novel radar technology to construct highly-directional wireless channels dynamically.
Task C: 	To realize an integrated WEC prototype and demonstrate its performance in a wave tank.
This interdisciplinary project will be carried out collaboratively by three investigators — two from mechanical engineering and one from electrical engineering.  One expert from the offshore energy industry will serve as the consultant in our team.

CONGRANT.TITLE: RUI: Wave-energy-converter pitch dynamics and its coupling with heave and surge
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT: We propose to advance the exploration in wave-energy-convertor (WEC) hydrodynamics by focusing on wave interaction with WECs.  A WEC is a general means used to harvest energy from ocean waves.  The overall objective of this project is to better understand the flow physics of the nonlinear wave interaction with free-floating WECs.  The fundamental understanding gained will guide the development of a proof-of-concept WEC that: (i) uses angular oscillation (pitch) to harvest wave energy, and (ii) demonstrates the potential to generate low-cost electricity.  In this project, we will integrate research with undergraduate education.  Five research tasks and three education tasks will be carried out in parallel throughout the duration of this project.  The research aspect of this project has a focus on WEC hydrodynamics that is to be conducted experimentally in a wave tank.  The education component involves participation of both undergraduate and local high-school students and improvement of our engineering curriculum.

CONGRANT.ABSTRACT: We propose to advance the exploration in wave-energy-convertor (WEC) hydrodynamics by focusing on wave interaction with WECs.  A WEC is a general means used to harvest energy from ocean waves.  The overall objective of this project is to better understand the flow physics of the nonlinear wave interaction with free-floating WECs.  The fundamental understanding gained will guide the development of a proof-of-concept WEC that: (i) uses angular oscillation to harvest wave energy, and (ii) demonstrates the potential to generate low-cost electricity.  In this project, we will integrate research with undergraduate education.  Five research tasks and three education tasks will be carried out in parallel throughout the duration of this project.  The research aspect of this project includes experimental exploration to be conducted in a wave tank under various wave conditions using a variety of WEC models.  The education component involves participation of both undergraduate and local high-school students and improvement of our engineering curriculum.

CONGRANT.TITLE: SEP Collaborative: A system to harvest wave energy for low-cost electricity
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT: This research proposes an innovative approach for energy harvesting from ocean waves at a low cost.  It employs brand-new wave farm architecture, in which free-floating and fully-encapsulated wave energy convertors (WECs) are deployed in the ocean around a base station.  The WECs convert wave energy into electricity.  The scavenged electricity is transmitted to the base station wirelessly and then delivered from the base station to an onshore power station via an undersea cable.  The major objective of this research is to achieve WECs that can be easily deployed and that demand little maintenance in a lifespan of about six years.  Its success is expected to significantly lower the costs associated with wave energy scavenging, and further, to promote ocean waves as a competitive renewable energy source.  This interdisciplinary project will be carried out collaboratively by five PIs, one senior personnel, and one industrial consultant.

CONGRANT.TITLE: Collaborative Research: A wave energy harvesting system employing wireless power transmission
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT: This research proposes an innovative approach for energy harvesting from ocean waves.  It employs a brand-new wave farm architecture, in which free-floating and fully-encapsulated wave energy convertors (WECs) are deployed around a base station.  The WECs convert wave energy into electricity.  The scavenged electricity is transmitted to the base station wirelessly, and then delivered from the base station to an onshore power station via an undersea cable.  The major objective of this research is to achieve WECs that demand little maintenance in a lifespan of about six years.  Its success is expected to significantly relieve the high maintenance costs associated with wave energy scavenging devices, which constitute a bottleneck in the wave-energy industry.  This interdisciplinary project will be carried out collaboratively by four PIs  two from mechanical engineering at the University of Texas at Brownsville (UTB), and two from electrical engineering at the University of Texas at Arlington (UTA).

INTELLCONT.TITLE: Experimental characterization of cloth wetting for humidification-dehumidification desalination

INTELLCONT_AUTH.INSTITUTION: University of Texas Rio Grande Valley
University of Texas Rio Grand Valley

INTELLCONT.PUBLISHER: International Communications in Heat and Mass Transfer
INTELLCONT.ABSTRACT: A novel humidification technology for desalination in an environmentally friendly and sustainable way has been proposed and investigated in this work. It is based on cloth wetting, driven by a natural ocean environment, to enhance air humidification. The enabled humidifier serves as a key component in an ocean-situated humidification-dehumidification desalination system, which is directly powered by nature with zero electricity consumption and zero brine discharge. Two cloth wetting mechanisms—wicking and falling films—have been tested on a variety of woven and knitted cloths. The two mechanisms can seamlessly transition from one to another in the proposed humidifier, depending on ocean conditions – wicking in a calm sea or falling films in waves. Based on the cloth wetting characterization, some representative cloths have been tested in a model humidifier under simulated conditions. The testing results and further analysis show that, in comparison with a baseline case of no cloth wetting, wicking can double the freshwater production rate, and falling films can quintuple it. The promising results demonstrate great potential for cloth wetting in clean water production in a sustainable way.

INTELLCONT.TITLE: CFD Evaluation of the self-starting of a vertical-axis wave turbine and the related flow and load characteristics
INTELLCONT.ABSTRACT: Abstract The research and application of marine renewable energy have received much attention due to its potential to generate power with less emissions than traditional sources. Among various types of wave energy converters (WECs), research is still in its infancy for Vertical-Axis Wave Turbines. While the concept has been well adopted in the wind energy industry, the use of this technology for wave energy harvesting could meet challenges due to the reciprocal motion of surface waves. When previously tested, the wave turbine design showed promising spin-up and sustained rotation of the rotor in regular waves. This test encouraged detailed assessment of the self-starting process of the rotor in the present work. For numerical simulation, a Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) model following the Reynolds-Averaged Navier-Stokes framework was established. The model took various aspects into account, such as the influence of the numerical waves, the highly unsteady initial self-starting process, and the appropriate gridding strategy needed to suit a wide range of rotational speeds from near-zero to the quasi-steady, terminal speed of the rotor. The CFD model was applied to reveal detailed characteristics of the flow field and to evaluate the sensitivity of the self-starting process to different inertial properties and damping coefficients of the rotor. The simulation showed that the inertial properties of the rotor would only affect the efficiency of the self-starting process. In contrast, the damping coefficient could have a profound effect on the attained steady-state rotational speed, which has strong implication for the design of power-take-off. The methodology established in the present work will be invaluable for design optimization as the self-starting process is an important stage of the device operating in an ever-changing environment. The methodology is also transferrable to other types of renewable energy devices that are equipped with a self-started rotor.

INTELLCONT.TITLE: Wave energy converters with rigid hull encapsulation: A review

INTELLCONT_AUTH.INSTITUTION: University of Texas Rio Grande Valley

INTELLCONT.ABSTRACT: Ocean wave energy has a great potential in mitigating energy and sustainability crises of the 21st century. The lack of mature and cost-competitive wave energy converter (WEC) technologies, however, has become a major roadblock for WEC products entering the marketplace. A harsh ocean environment, which includes extreme waves, strong biological activities, and chemical transformations, adds to the maintenance cost and survivability of WECs. Among various types of WEC technologies, WECs with rigid hull encapsulation offer an effective means against such environmental challenges. Using a sole rigid hull to encapsulate an entire WEC except for power cables and mooring lines, the hull creates a robust and watertight protection to the WEC and permits a relatively simple WEC design. This review provides a comprehensive analysis on existing WEC technologies employing such rigid hull encapsulation. The review topics cover technologies and working principles, power generation mechanisms, control strategies, mooring schemes, experimental studies, as well as technology readiness levels and development trends. Some future research considerations are suggested in addressing some common challenges. As an effort to present a global view of this particular type of WECs, the review is expected to benefit future WEC developments employing rigid hull encapsulation.

INTELLCONT.TITLE: Feasibility analysis of a wave powered autonomous underwater vehicle

INTELLCONT_AUTH.INSTITUTION: University of Texas Rio Grande Valley

INTELLCONT.ABSTRACT: An autonomous underwater vehicle (AUV) powered by renewable energy would enable it to extend endurance and forward presence with no logistics tail for fuel. A wave powered concept AUV is proposed and analyzed for this purpose. The AUV is in a torpedo shape and employs a fully hull-encapsulated mass-spring-damper system as its power take-off (PTO) unit. While in the recharging mode, the AUV surfaces and converts wave energy for electricity. Considering the AUV of a common size, our analysis indicates that resonance of the AUV and/or its PTO, to be excited by ocean waves, becomes impossible in typical ocean conditions. Then by making the AUV almost fully submerged to eliminate its intrinsic resonant nature and by applying some realistic constraints, the AUV’s power generation capability without resonance is characterized. Our simulation results show that the AUV is still capable of generating power at a decent level in a wide range of the wave frequency upon optimization. Some guiding principles have been established for AUV design of this type.

INTELLCONT.TITLE: Bio-inspired micromachined volumetric flow sensor with a big dynamic range for intravenous systems
INTELLCONT.ABSTRACT: Real-time monitoring of drug delivery in an intravenous infusion system can prevent injury caused by improper drug doses. As the medicine must be administered into the vein at different rates and doses in different people, an ideal intravenous infusion system requires both a low flow rate and large dynamic range monitoring. In this study, a bio-inspired and micromachined volumetric flow sensor is presented for the biomedical application of an intravenous system. This was realized by integrating two sensing units with different sensitivities on one silicon die to achieve a large dynamic range of the volumetric flow rate. The sensor was coated with a parylene layer for waterproofing and biocompatibility purposes. A new packaging scheme incorporating a silicon die into a flow channel was employed to demonstrate the working prototype. The test results indicate that the sensor can detect a volumetric flow rate as low as 2 mL/h, and its dynamic range is from 2 mL/h to 200 mL/h. The sensor performed better than the other two commercial sensors for low-flow detection. The high sensitivity, low cost, and small size of this flow sensor make it promising for intravenous applications.

Tailoring the viscosity of water and ethylene glycol based TiO2 nanofluids
CFD Investigation of Wave Energy Convertor with Hydrofoil Blades under Various Oscillating Wave Conditions
INTELLCONT.ABSTRACT: Ocean waves are a rich source of renewable energy with a much higher power density than winds. Various wave energy converter (WEC) technologies have been proposed or are under development. In this study, we developed a numerical model and analyzed the rotational motion of a lift-type rotor under steady and oscillating flow conditions. The numerical model was validated by experimental data in steady flows. Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) analysis was performed to identify the major contribution of the oscillating frequency in terms of vortices generated in the flow field. A comparative study was also performed by comparing all the cases in terms of the energy conversion efficiency under different wave conditions. It turns out that the energy conversion efficiency peaks in steady flows, and decreases with the increasing oscillating frequency in unsteady flows. Such a trend is highly due to the increased dissipation because of the oscillation. Under the examined conditions, a minimum energy conversion efficiency of 1.6% is predicted. The rotation speed of the rotor fluctuates in both steady and oscillating flows, with the average value in steady flows higher than that in oscillating flows. It is expected that the simulation results can contribute to the wave energy community, especially when the rotor design and optimization is required.

INTELLCONT.TITLE: Experimental study of a lift-type wave energy converter rotor in a freewheeling mode
INTELLCONT.ABSTRACT: In pursuit of energy harvesting from ocean waves, our recent progress on studying wave interaction with a lift-type rotor is discussed in this paper. The particular focus is on characterization of the rotor’s unidirectional responsiveness in waves. The rotor consists of six hydrofoil blades in two sets. One blade set has three blades laid out as a vertical-axis wind turbine of the Darrieus type. The other blade set has three blades configured like a Wells turbine. In combination, the formed rotor can be driven by flows in any direction to perform unidirectional rotation about its vertically mounted shaft. This unidirectional responsiveness of the rotor also holds in waves, making the rotor an effective device for wave energy conversion. For parametric study of the rotor, hydrofoil blades using different cross sectional profiles and chord lengths have been employed to configure the rotor. The rotor was then tested in a wave flume under various wave conditions in a freewheeling mode. Experimental results were analyzed and discussed. The yielded research findings will greatly enhance the fundamental understanding on the rotor performance in waves, and effectively guide the prototype rotor development for practical applications.

INTELLCONT.TITLE: NUMERICAL SIMULATION OF WAVE ENERGY CONVERTER WITH HYDROFOIL BLADES UNDER VARIOUS WAVE CONDITIONS
INTELLCONT.PUBLISHER: ASME 2019 13th International Conference on Energy Sustainability
INTELLCONT.ABSTRACT: Ocean wave is a rich source of renewable energy with much higher power density than winds. Various WEC technologies have been proposed or are under development. In this study, we developed a 2-dimensional (2D) model and analyzed the rotational motion of the lift-type rotor’s blade under steady flow and unsteady flow. The numerical model was validated by experiments under steady flow. Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) analysis was performed to identify the major contribution of frequency in terms of vortexes generated in the flow field. A comparative study was also performed by comparing all the cases in terms of energy conversion efficiency under different wave conditions. It turns out that the efficiency of energy conversion has a maximum value in the steady flow, while the efficiency for unsteady flow keeps decreasing, therefore this is highly due to the increased dissipation because of the oscillating. When the flow is oscillating, the rotational speed of the rotor under periodic condition is lower than the rotational velocity with steady flow, and a curve fitting was performed in this study to predict the periodic average rotational speed. We conclude that for oscillating flow a minimum of 1.6% energy conversion efficiency can be expected, but it may vary for the actual ocean waves. It is expected the current 2D simulation results can contribute to the wave energy community, especially when the rotor design and optimization is required.
